article_text:
Taking a cue from various attempts to breathe cinematic life into the Mortal Kombat franchise, including one earlier this year, another oldie but goodie from the heyday and beloved universe of video game classics is taking a swing at appealing to new generations of fans who weren’t even born when the iconic game Street Fighter first appeared in 1987.

In addition to various animated and TV series takes, there have been a couple of big-screen attempts, the most notable in 1994 with Jean-Claude Van Damme’s Street Fighter which was a box office hit. However, the 2009 attempt, Street Fighter: The Legend Of Chun-Li, was a miserable flop. Now with Legendary and the game’s creator Capcom teaming up we have a new and perhaps the most elaborate reboot yet. Whether anyone was asking for it is another question.

Sprinkled with supporting roles for bigger names like Jason Momoa and Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson, and set for sweet nostalgia smack in the heart of Street Fighter’s golden era of the early 1990s, director and co-writer Kitao Sakurai has made sure there is a certain affectionate cheesy cartoonish quality that makes this 2026 edition look like it was made in 1993, the year it takes place. Everything is heightened here; the action, the acting, the visuals, the stunts, and even in a nod to its ‘toon cousins, the hand-drawn animation that opens the movie and reappears in flashback form to tell the origin story of its two main protagonists, Ryu ( Andrew Koji ) and Ken Masters ( Noah Centineo ), and their Miyagi-like mentor Master Gouken whose wise words pepper the proceedings throughout.

Growing up brothers and fighting aficionados, Ryu and Ken split in 1987, the year of the first World Warrior Tournament. Ryu became the quiet triumphant fighter while Ken failed to make the tournament of champions, losing most of his self worth and now six years later a shadow of his former self, prone to tacky endorsements and minor celebrity. Ryu knows the real truth about Ken but keeps it to himself and has become a loner, a man purposely hiding from his past cooking up a new identity in the food world.

Neither had any expectations to ever see each other again, much less get into the ring, but the evil and manipulative boss of the Shandaloo organization, Lord M. Bison (David Dastmalchian, going as far over the top as you can possibly go) has plans to revive the World Warrior Tournament and needs both Ryu and Ken to make a comeback. Of course this is all a front for more devious plans, but it is up to recruiter Chun-Li (newcomer Callina Liang ) to get them on board against all odds. She is the shrewd sort of talent agent here out to sign up an all-star line up of street-fighting legends, but she has her own secret motive and that is to kill Bison, the man responsible for the death of her father. Working for him is her ticket to do just that and so the reunion, like something out of The Sunshine Boys, brings reluctant Ryu and Ken back together. It is all ultimately about brotherly love.

The main event is World Warrior Tournament II and it is loaded with a “who’s who gonna kill you,” presided over by very loud M.C. Doc Sauvage (a very loud Eric André). We will eventually meet stoic and confident 50 Cent’s lethal boxer Balrog; Dutch Giant and one-man wrecking crew Zangief (Olivier Richters); yoga-style martial artist Dhalsim (Vidyut Jammwal); platinum blonde flat-topped Guile (WWE’s Cody Rhodes); the spirited Momoa’s Hulk-like electrifying fan favorite Blanka; imposing Akuma (WWE’s Joe “Roman Reigns” Anoai); and more. And then flooding the danger zone are the associates of Bison including masked terror Vega (Orville Peck) and the other female warriors Juli (martial arts star Rayna Vallandingham) and Cammy aka Killer Bee (Mel Jarnson).

Both main stars do well and are convincing fighters, especially Koji, who actually manages some levels of depth for Ryu. In for some comic relief is the amusing manager of Ken, Dan Hibiki (sharp comedian Andrew Schulz), who adds a much needed dose of anti-testosterone in this guy who has a sweet sort of relationship with the insecure Ken. The real star here may just be stunt choreographer Jon Valera who gets to show his stuff, particularly in a burlesque free-for-all in which just about everyone appears — or so it seems.

Impressive moves aside, if anything this whole enterprise feels more like a comic book movie than martial arts showcase. Its PG-13 rating tells us that the action and numerous fights will not be going the violent ways of John Wick, so it is best to have a love for simpler times. It is all very safe and true to what core Street Fighter fans, many now knocking on eligibility for AARP, will likely appreciate more than anyone else.

Producers are Mary Parent, Cale Boyter, Momoa, Stefan Makhoul and Takayuki Nakayama.

true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅道格拉斯的画作来自北卡罗来纳州格林斯伯勒的贝内特学院（Bennett College），该校是美国仅有的两所历史悠久的非裔女子学院之一。其拍卖所得将用于支持包括女性健康公平在内的各项倡议。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅画势必为道格拉斯创下新的拍卖纪录。他的拍卖最高纪录仅为600,000美元，是在2008年由纽约斯旺画廊（Swann Galleries）拍卖其小幅画作《Building More Stately Mansions》（1944年）时创下的，当时的最高估价为150,000美元（斯旺画廊包揽了该艺术家拍卖成交价前10名中的6个）。《哈丽特·塔布曼》宽达6英尺，其尺寸比他在公开拍卖中的任何顶级作品都要宏大得多。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "苏富比副主席兼当代艺术部主管大卫·加尔珀林（David Galperin）在接受《ARTnews》电话采访时表示：“关于亚伦·道格拉斯的市场，情况是这些画作根本就不存在，句号。最具代表性的画作在近二十年前被提供过。那是在硬质纤维板上，高约20英寸。当然，自那以后，现代艺术市场已经发展，从诺曼·刘易斯（Norman Lewis）、雅各布·劳伦斯（Jacob Lawrence）到罗马尔·比登（Romare Bearden）等艺术家都得到了重新评估。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他继续说道：“我们从未见过[道格拉斯的]重要作品现身拍卖行，因为它们实在、实在是太稀少了。有一些作品通过私下洽购售出，价格超过了我们的低端估价，并直接进入了现代艺术博物馆和国家美术馆等博物馆。这些机构都收购了重要的作品，但那只是在过去15年里。考虑到这件作品的重要性，如果我们看到全球各大博物馆竞逐这件作品，我也不会感到惊讶。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Harriet-Tubman-Installed-in-College-Residence-Hall.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "正在贝内特学院展出的亚伦·道格拉斯作品《哈丽特·塔布曼》（1931年）。图片来源：Bennett College", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "出生于堪萨斯州的道格拉斯在20世纪20年代搬到哈莱姆，并成为了哈莱姆文艺复兴时期的杰出人物，同期的艺术家还包括阿奇博尔德·J·莫特利（Archibald J. Motley）、奥古斯塔·萨维奇（Augusta Savage）、黑尔·伍德鲁夫（Hale Woodruff）和詹姆斯·范德泽（James Van Der Zee）等。正如香黛·罗宾逊（Shantay Robinson）为《ARTnews》撰文所指出的那样，这个定义时代的文化运动希望通过文学、音乐、绘画、摄影和思想来创造一种新的非裔身份，她并指出道格拉斯受到非洲艺术形式的启发，并用它们创造出了堪比毕加索和马蒂斯等欧洲现代主义者的艺术。她在谈到道格拉斯时写道：“通过将形象平面化、使用大胆的几何形状、绘制剪影以及采用非洲母题，他的作品定义了这场运动的视觉艺术。”哲学家阿兰·洛克（Alain Locke）曾称道格拉斯是“美国黑人艺术之父”。", "links": [{"text": "wrote", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/feature/what-was-the-harlem-renaissance-1234733148/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "道格拉斯这幅充满戏剧性的画作描绘了塔布曼站在一小块高地上，在一旁众人的注视下挣断链条；道格拉斯将他的创作主题描述为“一位挣脱奴役枷锁并向着新的一天奋勇前行的英雄领袖”。这幅画呼应了欧仁·德拉克罗瓦（Eugène Delacroix）1830年的杰作《自由引导人民》（Liberty Leading the People）的构图，该画藏于巴黎卢浮宫。围绕在塔布曼身边的有正在自己土地上劳作的男子，也有正在读书的年轻女性。《哈丽特·塔布曼》与道格拉斯在短短三年后创作的最著名作品《黑人生活面面观》（Aspects of Negro Life）在某些形式特质上有相通之处。", "links": [{"text": "Liberty Leading the People", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists/liberty-leading-the-people-eugene-delacroix-romanticism-1234758060/"}, {"text": "Aspects of Negro Life", "url": "https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/634ad849-7832-309e-e040-e00a180639bb"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅画描绘了这位著名的废奴主义者和社会活动家，她在1849年自己逃离奴隶制后，通过被称为“地下铁路”的秘密网络，冒险深入南方州开展了大约13次生死攸关的任务，营救了大约70名被奴役的人，其中一些是她的家人和朋友。她在南北战争期间曾担任联邦军队的武装侦察员和间谍，后来还在争取妇女选举权的运动中发挥了作用。（女演员辛西娅·艾里沃（Cynthia Erivo）在2019年的故事片《哈丽特》中饰演了她，影评人欧文·格莱伯曼（Owen Gleiberman）曾评价该片对她的刻画“带着一种悲伤的愤怒”。）", "links": [{"text": "observed", "url": "https://variety.com/2019/film/reviews/harriet-review-cynthia-erivo-1203330489/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Aaron-Douglas.jpg?w=400", "alt": "非裔美国画家亚伦·道格拉斯（1899 - 1979）的肖像。他曾长期担任菲斯克大学教授，也是哈莱姆文艺复兴运动的代表人物，摄于田纳西州画架前，约1970年代。（图片由 Robert Abbott Sengstacke/Getty Images 拍摄）", "caption": "亚伦·道格拉斯在田纳西州的画架前作画，约1970年代。图片来源：Robert Abbott Sengstacke/Getty Images", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝内特学院代理校长罗纳德·卡特（Ronald Carter）在电话采访中谈到这幅画时说：“它充满力量。审视这些象征意义令人惊叹，作为一个非裔美国人，我真的想说：太棒了！当我看到它时，我心里想的是：太棒了！我们能有今天，是因为哈丽特·塔布曼有远见。我们之所以成为现在的我们，是因为我们能够努力工作，为我们的未来创造可能。我们身处此地，是因为我们是社会活动家。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卡特在14岁时首次访问了这所学校，他接着说道：“看着它，总结了我自己在50年代到60年代以及民权运动中成长经历。如果你看着它，看到链条的断裂、人们迈向未来以及自由可能意味着什么，所有这些都是我们机构不可或缺的一部分。它代表了我们最好的一面。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自从2007年由堪萨斯大学斯彭斯艺术博物馆（Spencer Museum of Art）组织了一场巡回回顾展以来，道格拉斯的艺术作品一直在缓缓受到更多关注。他的作品还显著亮相于大都会艺术博物馆2024年的展览“哈莱姆文艺复兴与跨大西洋现代主义”（The Harlem Renaissance and Transatlantic Modernism），该馆于2015年首次购入这位艺术家的纤维板油画。国家美术馆则于2014年购入了这位艺术家的两幅画作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "芝加哥慈善家阿尔弗雷德·K·斯特恩（Alfred K. Stern）为该学院的餐厅委托创作了这件道格拉斯作品。该学院于1873年（即《解放宣言》发表十年后）创立于一家教堂的地下室。它于1926年成为一所女子学院，并与亚特兰大的斯佩尔曼学院（Spelman College）一同，成为仅有的两所全女子历史上的黑人大学（HBCU）。", "links": [{"text": "Spelman College", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/atlanta-university-center-black-art-history-scholarship-1234676015/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅画作已在北卡罗来纳艺术博物馆（North Carolina Museum of Art）悬挂了20年。此前，由于该校没有博物馆，认为无法妥善保管它，因此将其送到了那里。卡特表示，出售这幅画的决定是在经过两年多的审议后作出的。所得款项将用于支持该校未来的发展，包括扩大在1月启动的妇女健康倡议（Women’s Health Initiative），以解决医疗保健差距并促进妇女的健康公平。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝内特学院的校友被称为“贝内特佳丽”（Bennett Belles），其中包括已故艺术家贝弗莉·布坎南（Beverly Buchanan）；美国国会女议员阿尔玛·亚当斯（Alma Adams）；和平队（Peace Corps）历史上第一位女性兼第一位非洲裔美国人局长卡罗琳·佩顿（Carolyn Payton）；以及马萨诸塞州首位担任助理总检察长的非洲裔美国女性格伦多拉·普特南（Glendora Putnam）。1955年，贝内特成为美国第一所有黑人女性威拉·比特里斯·普莱尔（Willa Beatrice Player）领导的四年制大学。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在其任职期间，普莱尔曾于1958年当地全国有色人种协进会（NAACP）分会邀请马丁·路德·金（Martin Luther King, Jr.）来到该市时，欢迎他在校园发表演讲。学生们还在格林斯博罗组织了关键的民权静坐抗议活动。“人们并不知情，但他们正是在贝内特的校园里拟定了这一行动计划，”卡特说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本月，新一批“贝内特佳丽”在当地选举委员会拒绝在贝内特、北卡罗来纳大学格林斯博罗分校（UNC Greensboro）以及北卡罗来纳农工大学（North Carolina A&T）的校园内设立往届选举季曾开放的早期投票点后，徒步约45分钟前往投票地点在该州进行早期投票，从而登上了各大媒体头条。", "links": [{"text": "made headlines", "url": "https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/north-carolina-t-unc-greensboro-014543629.html"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卡特补充道：“我们所做的一切，不仅代表着传统与历史，更代表着赋权给那些将以其优雅、坚韧与成长继续撼动这个国家根基的贝内特佳丽。”", "translated": true}]

article_text:
A monumental painting by a leading artist of the Harlem Renaissance , showing a legendary figure from the struggle for African American liberation, will come to auction at Sotheby’s New York next month.

Aaron Douglas ’s painting Harriet Tubman (1931) is expected to sell for between $2.5 million–$3.5 million, the highest estimate ever placed on a work by Douglas. The painting will go to the block as part of the house’s marquee modern art auction on November 18.

The first example by the artist ever to be featured in such a high-profile sale, it will go on public view at the house’s New York headquarters beginning November 7. The work carries a house guarantee, Sotheby’s confirmed to ARTnews .

The Douglas painting is on offer from the holdings of Bennett College, in Greensboro, North Carolina, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US. Proceeds from its sale will be used to support initiatives including women’s health equity.

The painting is bound to set a new record for Douglas, whose auction high stands at just $600,000, achieved against a $150,000 high estimate in 2008, when the small painting Building More Stately Mansions (1944) sold at New York’s Swann Galleries, which is responsible for six of the artist’s top 10 prices at auction. Measuring six feet wide, Harriet Tubman is dramatically larger than any of his top works at public sales.

“The thing about the market for Aaron Douglas is the paintings don’t exist, period,” said David Galperin, Sotheby’s vice chairman and head of contemporary art, told ARTnews in a phone interview. “The most significant painting was offered nearly two decades ago. It was on Masonite and it’s about 20 inches high. Of course, since then, the market for modern art has evolved, and artists from Norman Lewis and Jacob Lawrence to Romare Bearden have been reappraised.“

He continued, “We haven’t seen a major work [by Douglas] come to auction ever because they are so, so rare. There have been a few that have sold privately at prices in excess of our low estimate, that have gone directly to museums like the Museum of Modern Art and the National Gallery of Art. These institutions have all acquired important works, but only in the past 15 years. I wouldn’t be surprised, given the importance of this work, if we see major museums globally compete for this piece.”

Kansas-born Douglas moved to Harlem in the 1920s and became a prominent figure in the Harlem Renaissance, which also included artists like Archibald J. Motley, Augusta Savage, Hale Woodruff, and James Van Der Zee. The era-defining cultural movement looked to create a new Black identity through literature, music, painting, photography, and thought, as Shantay Robinson wrote for ARTnews , noting that Douglas was inspired by African forms and used them to create art comparable to that of European modernists like Picasso and Matisse. “By flattening his figures, using bold geometric shapes, painting silhouettes, and employing African motifs,” she wrote of Douglas, “his work defined the visual art of the movement.” Philosopher Alain Locke would call Douglas “the father of Black American Art.”

Douglas’s dramatic painting shows Tubman on an elevated bit of turf, breaking a chain as others look on; Douglas described his subject as “a heroic leader breaking the shackles of bondage and pressing on toward a new day.” The painting echoes the composition of Eugène Delacroix’s 1830 masterpiece Liberty Leading the People , which hangs in the Louvre in Paris. Among the figures around Tubman is a man working his own land and a young woman reading a book. Harriet Tubman shares some formal qualities with Douglas’s most famous work, Aspects of Negro Life , painted just three years later.

The painting depicts the famed abolitionist and social activist who, after escaping slavery herself in 1849, went on some 13 death-defying missions back into the Southern states to rescue about 70 enslaved people, some of them her family and friends, via the network known as the Underground Railroad. She would serve as an armed scout and spy for the Union Army during the Civil War and would later also play a role in the movement for women’s suffrage. (Actress Cynthia Erivo depicted her in the 2019 feature film Harriet , which film critic Owen Gleiberman observed as a depiction “with a mournful fury.”)

“It’s powerful,” Bennett College’s acting president Ronald Carter said of the painting in a phone interview. “It’s awesome to look at the symbolism, and for me as an African American to actually say, Yes! When I looked at it I went, Yes! We are where we are because Harriet Tubman had a vision. We are who we are because we were able to do hard work to make things happen for our future. We are where we are because we are social activists.”

Carter, who first visited the school when he was 14 years old, continued, “Looking at it summed up my experience growing up in the ’50s and into the ’60s and the civil rights movement. If you look at it and see the breaking of the chains and people going into the future and what it can mean to be free, all these things are integral to our institutions. It represents the best of what we are.”

Since a 2007 traveling retrospective, which was organized by the Spencer Museum of Art at the University of Kansas, Douglas’s art has been slowly on the rise. His work also prominently featured in the 2024 exhibition “The Harlem Renaissance and Transatlantic Modernism” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, which first acquired an oil on masonite by the artist in 2015. The National Gallery of Art acquired two paintings by the artist in 2014.

Chicago philanthropist Alfred K. Stern commissioned the Douglas work for a dining hall at the college, which was founded in a church basement in 1873, just a decade after the Emancipation Proclamation. It became a women’s college in 1926, and, with Atlanta’s Spelman College , is one of just two all-women HBCUs.

The painting has hung for two deades at the North Carolina Museum of Art, where it went after the school, which does not have a museum, determined it couldn’t responsibly care for it. The decision to sell the painting comes after more than two years of deliberation, Carter said. The proceeds will support the school’s future growth, including expanding its Women’s Health Initiative, which was launched in January to addres healthcare disparities and advances health equity for women.

Bennett College’s alumnae, known as the Bennett Belles, include late artist Beverly Buchanan; US congresswoman Alma Adams; Carolyn Payton, the first woman and first African American director of the Peace Corps; and Glendora Putnam, the first African American woman to serve as assistant attorney general in Massachusetts. In 1955, Bennett became the first four-year college in the US to be led by a Black woman, Willa Beatrice Player.

During her tenure, Player welcomed Martin Luther King, Jr. to speak on campus in 1958 when the local chapter of the NAACP invited him to the city. Students also organized key civil rights sit-in protests in Greensboro. “People don’t know, but they worked out that plan of action right here on Bennett’s campus,” Carter said.

A new set of Bennett Belles made headlines this month when they marched about 45 minutes to a polling location to cast ballots in the state’s early voting after the county board of elections denied early polling locations on the campuses of Bennett, UNC Greensboro, and North Carolina A&T that have been open in past election seasons.

Carter added, “Everything about what we are doing represents not only the legacy and history but empowering the figure with Bennett Belles who will continue to shake the foundations of this country through their grace, grit and growth.”
excerpt_original: The painting, by the “father of Black American art,” shows an emancipator sometimes referred to as “Moses.”

"这部低成本的英国纪录片正处于高歌猛进之中，即将首次在美国上映，但其登上大银幕的历程漫长而曲折。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "影片讲述了德文郡的两位邻居农场主，巧合的是两人都叫德里克（Derek）。其中一位德里克·高（Derek Gow）是一位重野化保护主义者，另一位德里克·班伯里（Derek Banbury）则是一位集约化奶农。两人对同名同姓的对方有着天然的不信任，但勉强愿意听取对方的意见。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "威沙特曾因 BBC 和 Apple TV 精彩的《9/11：总统战情室内幕》（9/11: Inside the President’s War {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部纪录片记录了两位德里克在日常生活的同时贯彻他们截然相反的愿景。高是一位重野化倡导者，他正在采取激进的措施，例如在农田里引入野猪，并且他希望走得更远，说服当地人允许狼群重返英国。班伯里则是一位传统农场主，真正关心的主要是维持生计。慢慢地，有时伴随着巨大的戏剧性，他们的观点逐渐向彼此靠拢，《德里克大战德里克》绝不偏袒任何一方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "威沙特认为，这部纪录片成功的关键确实在于主角之间的关系以及他们各自的性格，他将其形容为“精彩且颇具原型意义，但也出人意料”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他补充道：“关于这样的人的纪录片并不多。我们生活在一个如此两极分化的世界里，以至于我们认为两个观点对立的人会在生活的方方面面闹翻，并不再说话。但完全有可能在生活的一个方面产生分歧，而当你的拖拉机陷住时，依然会给邻居打电话。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在由汤姆·克鲁斯（Tom article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Welcome to Global Breakouts , Deadline’s strand in which, each fortnight, we shine a spotlight on the TV shows and films killing it in their local territories. The industry is as globalized as it’s ever been, but breakout hits are appearing in pockets of the world all the time and it can be hard to keep track… So, we’re going to do the hard work for you.", "links": [{"text": "Global Breakouts", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/global-breakouts/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We’re in the UK this week spotlighting an environmental documentary about warring neighbors that is gaining big traction. With a U.S. premiere coming shortly, Derek vs Derek has taken years to get to the big screen. Its exec producer Adam Wishart sets out its journey below.", "links": [{"text": "Derek vs Derek", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/derek-vs-derek/"}, {"text": "Adam Wishart", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/adam-wishart/"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Related Stories"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Hunkkaar-1000-e1791557997508.jpg?w=300", "alt": "'Hunkkaar'", "caption": "", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "The \"Algorithm Breaking\" 'Hunkkaar' Has Challenged Indian Audiences On The Limits Of Procedural TV - And Their Own Beliefs", "links": [{"text": "The \"Algorithm Breaking\" 'Hunkkaar' Has Challenged Indian Audiences On The Limits Of Procedural TV - And Their Own Beliefs", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/10/hunkkaar-india-jiohotstar-series-global-breakout-1237150945/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Pedro-Pina-1.jpg?w=300", "alt": "Pedro Pina", "caption": "", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "International Insider: The Final Edinburgh... Or Is It?; Int'l Oscar Race Begins", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/08/international-insider-final-edinburgh-tv-festival-1237061772/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Name: Derek vs Derek Country: UK Producer: The Slate Works & Damer Films Distributor: CAT&Docs For fans of: Wilding", "links": [{"text": "The Slate Works", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/the-slate-works/"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Watch on Deadline"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Many years in the making, Derek vs Derek started life as a story of rewilding and arrived in cinemas as something quite different, a “universal” tale of warring neighbors who nevertheless never stop learning from each other, says the film’s exec producer, Adam Wishart."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The low-budget British documentary is riding on a high and is about to screen in the U.S. for the first time, but its journey to the big screen has been long and winding."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The movie follows two neighboring farmers in Devon, enjoyably both called Derek, one of whom, Derek Gow, is a rewilding conservationist, and the other, Derek Banbury, an intensive dairy farmer. Both have a natural distrust of their namesake, but are just about willing to hear them out."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wishart, a BAFTA nominee for the BBC and Apple TV’s fantastic 9/11: Inside the President’s War Room, lives in Devon, a short journey from Gow’s farm. He became aware of Gow and his work some time ago when he was advising on community regeneration."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/DEREKS-ARK-008.jpg?w=300", "alt": "", "caption": "Derek Gow Joss Barratt", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wishart was told a director, James Dawson, had been following Gow for some years in order to make a rewilding documentary similar to 2023 hit Wilding . He “tried to get the film commissioned and even used every piece of TV industry capital I had,” but Wishart kept running into brick walls. He felt something was missing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I was supportive [of Dawson’s vision], but a little sceptical,” says Wishart. “Then he told me that, whenever he stayed with Derek Gow, Derek would point him towards the Banburys and tell him to go and have breakfast with them. Suddenly, it became apparent that there was a lovely film about their relationship and their two different visions.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wishart knew this was more than a kernel of an idea and Dawson already had plenty footage, but funding was tricky to come by. In the end, money flowed in via a grant from the Redford Center foundation plus crowdfunding. “We’ve made it with a tiny budget, drawing favors from across the industry, with the whole endeavour held together by sticky back plastic and paperclips,” says Wishart, whose production house The Slate Works produced Derek vs Derek alongside Damer Films, with CAT&Docs handling international sales. While “getting documentaries off the ground has always been difficult,” Wishart notes that “it’s harder than ever to do something that doesn’t have an obvious hook – an anniversary, a major event or a famous celebrity.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Testing the protagonist"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/DEREKS-ARK-425-e1793094798824.jpg?w=300", "alt": "", "caption": "Derek Banbury Joss Barratt", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The doc sees the Dereks execute their opposing visions while going about their day-to-day lives. Gow is a rewilder who is taking drastic measures like introducing wild boars to his farmland, and he wants to go even further by convincing locals to allow wolves to return to the UK. Banbury is a traditional farmer who is really about making ends meet. Slowly, and at times with great drama, their outlooks move closer towards each other, and Derek vs Derek by no means takes sides."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wishart feels the key to the doc’s success is really in the protagonists’ relationship and their individual characters, which he describes as “brilliant and rather archetypal, but also unexpected.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“There aren’t many documentaries about people like them,” he adds. “We live in such a polarized world that we assume two people with opposing views are going to fall out over every aspect of their lives and never speak again. But it’s perfectly possible to disagree about one aspect of your life and still call your neighbor if your tractor gets stuck.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Speaking a few weeks after the launch of Tom Cruise-starring satirical polemic Digger, Wishart feels docs and features about this subject matter have become overly preachy."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“They make one group of people feel that their life choices are wonderful, while alienating another group,” he adds. “I thought [ Derek vs Derek ] was interesting because making a film that sits with only one protagonist can be problematic. It can feel like an ‘NGO film’ or piece of advocacy without much edge. article_text:
Welcome to Global Breakouts , Deadline’s strand in which, each fortnight, we shine a spotlight on the TV shows and films killing it in their local territories. The industry is as globalized as it’s ever been, but breakout hits are appearing in pockets of the world all the time and it can be hard to keep track… So, we’re going to do the hard work for you.

We’re in the UK this week spotlighting an environmental documentary about warring neighbors that is gaining big traction. With a U.S. premiere coming shortly, Derek vs Derek has taken years to get to the big screen. Its exec producer Adam Wishart sets out its journey below.

Related Stories

The "Algorithm Breaking" 'Hunkkaar' Has Challenged Indian Audiences On The Limits Of Procedural TV - And Their Own Beliefs

International Insider: The Final Edinburgh... Or Is It?; Int'l Oscar Race Begins

Name: Derek vs Derek Country: UK Producer: The Slate Works & Damer Films Distributor: CAT&Docs For fans of: Wilding

Watch on Deadline

Many years in the making, Derek vs Derek started life as a story of rewilding and arrived in cinemas as something quite different, a “universal” tale of warring neighbors who nevertheless never stop learning from each other, says the film’s exec producer, Adam Wishart.

The low-budget British documentary is riding on a high and is about to screen in the U.S. for the first time, but its journey to the big screen has been long and winding.

The movie follows two neighboring farmers in Devon, enjoyably both called Derek, one of whom, Derek Gow, is a rewilding conservationist, and the other, Derek Banbury, an intensive dairy farmer. Both have a natural distrust of their namesake, but are just about willing to hear them out.

Wishart, a BAFTA nominee for the BBC and Apple TV’s fantastic 9/11: Inside the President’s War Room, lives in Devon, a short journey from Gow’s farm. He became aware of Gow and his work some time ago when he was advising on community regeneration.

Wishart was told a director, James Dawson, had been following Gow for some years in order to make a rewilding documentary similar to 2023 hit Wilding . He “tried to get the film commissioned and even used every piece of TV industry capital I had,” but Wishart kept running into brick walls. He felt something was missing.

“I was supportive [of Dawson’s vision], but a little sceptical,” says Wishart. “Then he told me that, whenever he stayed with Derek Gow, Derek would point him towards the Banburys and tell him to go and have breakfast with them. Suddenly, it became apparent that there was a lovely film about their relationship and their two different visions.”

Wishart knew this was more than a kernel of an idea and Dawson already had plenty footage, but funding was tricky to come by. In the end, money flowed in via a grant from the Redford Center foundation plus crowdfunding. “We’ve made it with a tiny budget, drawing favors from across the industry, with the whole endeavour held together by sticky back plastic and paperclips,” says Wishart, whose production house The Slate Works produced Derek vs Derek alongside Damer Films, with CAT&Docs handling international sales. While “getting documentaries off the ground has always been difficult,” Wishart notes that “it’s harder than ever to do something that doesn’t have an obvious hook – an anniversary, a major event or a famous celebrity.”

Testing the protagonist

The doc sees the Dereks execute their opposing visions while going about their day-to-day lives. Gow is a rewilder who is taking drastic measures like introducing wild boars to his farmland, and he wants to go even further by convincing locals to allow wolves to return to the UK. Banbury is a traditional farmer who is really about making ends meet. Slowly, and at times with great drama, their outlooks move closer towards each other, and Derek vs Derek by no means takes sides.

Wishart feels the key to the doc’s success is really in the protagonists’ relationship and their individual characters, which he describes as “brilliant and rather archetypal, but also unexpected.”

“There aren’t many documentaries about people like them,” he adds. “We live in such a polarized world that we assume two people with opposing views are going to fall out over every aspect of their lives and never speak again. But it’s perfectly possible to disagree about one aspect of your life and still call your neighbor if your tractor gets stuck.”

Speaking a few weeks after the launch of Tom Cruise-starring satirical polemic Digger, Wishart feels docs and features about this subject matter have become overly preachy.

“They make one group of people feel that their life choices are wonderful, while alienating another group,” he adds. “I thought [ Derek vs Derek ] was interesting because making a film that sits with only one protagonist can be problematic. It can feel like an ‘NGO film’ or piece of advocacy without much edge. The protagonist isn’t really being tested.”

Gow and Banbury are now pals, and Wishart speaks to them frequently, with the pair appearing on Q&A panels around the country to support the movie. Wishart says the movie has made around £120,000 ($160,000) so far. According to the BFI, ticket sales for Derek vs Derek rose 114% week-on-week after launch. The movie has aired at festivals including in Thessaloniki and Zurich and will soon be given its U.S. premiere at New York’s Doc NY.

While Wishart is “not betting my mortgage on it,” he says “if the film can find a wider audience” by perhaps picking up U.S. distribution, thereby “beginning conversations about how we relate to the natural world and the food system, then more power to it.”

That, he thinks, is the beauty of Derek vs Derek, a “universal” story of grumpy neighbors that could maybe, whisper it, teach audiences a thing or two without them even realizing it.

article_text:
Shows

The Rhythm of a Dream: Qi Lei at Ben Brown Fine Arts

QI LEI ’s “Echoes of Day and Night” at Ben Brown Fine Arts, Hong Kong, 2026. Courtesy the artist and Ben Brown Fine Arts, Hong Kong.

Qi Lei Echoes of Day and Night Ben Brown Fine Arts Hong Kong Sep 12–Oct 31, 2026

How is the tempo of time marked? What pace do the hours keep to, when not measured by a clock? These questions have long fascinated Shanghai-based artist Qi Lei, and they receive sustained inquiry in his solo show “Echoes of Day and Night” at Ben Brown Fine Arts in Hong Kong. Inspired by traditional Western landscape conventions and the post-rock instrumentals of bands such as Godspeed You! Black Emperor, Qi examines how pictorial rhythm is orchestrated through oil, and how the painter—as composer—conducts the illusion of duration.

In Blue Sonata (2020), a canoe drifts through a jungle clearing across a hazy expanse of water. Qi’s framing evokes the compositional vignette of classic seascapes like Caspar David Friedrich’s Chalk Cliffs on Rügen (c. 1818), but strips the scene of its human presence down to a solitary, empty vessel. A palette of cool blues and greens calls to mind Frank Sinatra’s 1955 album In the Wee Small Hours , itself an exploration of the lonesome cadence of a nascent morning. Elements of abstraction materialize in the surrounds: vegetation blends into unknown shapes, intricate and insectile, contrasting with the spare brushstroke defining the distant hull. An illusory musicality permeates the tableau, moving steadily through the calm waters. Qi’s inquiry characterizes first light as an unhurried, elusive dream.

QI LEI ’s

Cozy Rest , 2020, oil on canvas, 160 x 160 cm (left); and

Blue Sonata , 2020, oil on canvas, 166 x 134 cm (right), at “Echoes of Day and Night,” Ben Brown Fine Arts, Hong Kong, 2026. Courtesy the artist and Ben Brown Fine Arts.

QI LEI ’s

Wind Listener’s Reverie 2 , 2024, oil on canvas, 200 x 150 cm (left);

Nighttime twilight , 2024, oil on canvas, 200 x 150 cm (middle); and

Hunting , 2021, oil on canvas, 200 x 150 cm (right), at “Echoes of Day and Night,” Ben Brown Fine Arts, Hong Kong, 2026. Courtesy the artist and Ben Brown Fine Arts.

Hunting (2021) develops these leitmotifs under opposite chromatic tones. A leopard sits atop its kill within a dense jungle, bathed in the rosy fingers of dusk. While the narrative recalls Henri Rousseau’s Le lion, ayant faim, se jette sur l’antilope (1898–1905), Qi resists Rousseau’s theatrical staging. Rather than occupying pride of place, the beasts merge into the surrounding thicket. Sponged smears of oil blur foliage and foreground into chimerical distortions—a subtractive handling designed to deconstruct figurative clarity. Channeling his fascination with musical structures, Qi charges the canvas with an abrupt stillness, like the pregnant pause that follows a high-intensity crescendo—as if the chase has only just ended.

The lone canoe recurs in Morning mist rises at dusk (2026), joined here by a figure whose torso blends into the surrounding branches, their face left blank. Like the leopard in Hunting , this human form serves the wider composition rather than commanding it; shape and color act as instruments within an ensemble. Temporal anonymity reaches its zenith: an indigo sky is fractured by a pink haze, the exact hour lost somewhere between daybreak and twilight. Even the figure’s gesture is unresolved: are they launching the craft or dragging it ashore? Caught between thresholds, a transitory tension holds rhythm at a standstill; what remains is insoluble suspense.

Walking through Qi’s show can feel like wading through a dream: colors are unnaturally vibrant, recognizable forms buckle, and the pulse of time is at once fluid and rigid. Brushwork operates as a metronome, spatial massing provides the percussive beats, and the hues of sunrise and sunset answer to one another. After all, what is dusk, if not an echo of the dawn?

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
excerpt_original: Through vibrant colors and figurative distortion, the artist investigates how time is constructed in a static medium. Harison Butler

article_text:
This week and next, Film Comment is reporting from the picturesque shores of the Lido, where the Venice Film Festival takes place each year. This year’s edition features new films by many major auteurs, including Werner Herzog, Lee Chang-dong, Tsai Ming-liang, and more.

For our third Podcast from the festival, Film Comment Co-Editor Devika Girish invited critics Jonathan Romney and Tim Grierson to share their reactions to The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias (2:38), director Sophie Fiennes’s latest collaboration with philosopher Slavoj Žižek, and Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger (14:36), Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace’s concert documentary following the band’s recent reunion tour. Finally, the three discussed one of the major standouts in the fest’s Competition section: May el-Toukhy‘s Woman Unknown (26:25).

Subscribe to Film Comment to stay up-to-date with all of our Venice 2026 coverage.

article_text:
Who knew that one of this year’s giddiest celebrations of filmmaking would be a movie where the stunt dummies are obvious, the dinosaur costumes are obviously homemade and you can literally see the strings on special effects shots?

That’s the joy of “ VelociPastor 2 ,” the long-awaited sequel to 2017’s “The VelociPastor.” The first film was a modern cult comedy classic made on a $36,000 budget, which followed the adventures of Doug Jones (Gregory James Cohan), a man of God who turns into a bloodthirsty dinosaur while he’s cleaning up his neighborhood from pimps and drug dealers, and his girlfriend Carol (Alyssa Kempinski).

Related Stories

Netflix's ‘The Blue Road’ Director Han Jun-hee on Why Playing It Safe Is the Real Risk

Netflix Touts International Success Amid Content Leadership Shake-Up, Eyes More Broadcaster Deals After TF1 and Globo Pacts

“VelociPastor 2” is even more ambitious, moving the action to “Italy” and spinning a yarn of a giallo -esque killer who is targeting area virgins. While the scope has widened, the low budget still keeps things charmingly ramshackle. Even after raising $118,297 on Kickstarter , all of the seams are still showing. But the effect is a tribute to low-budget filmmaking, poking fun at everything from wild inconsistencies that any script supervisor would have caught (the opening scene features Doug putting on a crucifix again and again) to wildly long pieces of exposition delivered via ADR.

Popular on Variety

The Sunday FilmQuest screening of “VelociPastor 2,” a festival known for attracting audiences filled with indie filmmakers, was primed to enjoy the movie and laughed boisterously throughout. Beyond the jabs at the joys and flaws of low-budget filmmaking, the movie is filled with plenty of other jokes in the spirit of “Airplane!” that kept spirits high.

There was also a sense of gratitude that so many of the jokes showed affection for the “let’s put on a show” enthusiasm that inspires both films. A frequent topic of discussion at the Provo, Utah-based festival has been the infiltration of AI in the industry, which is met with near-universal distrust and disinterest. In fact, one of the biggest applause points before every screening at the fest is a promise that the feature presentation doesn’t include AI.

But the joy of “VelociPastor 2” is the knowing silliness of low-budget filmmaking gone wrong, something that would be too complex to try to craft an AI prompt. Whether it’s miniatures that don’t show the true scope of Italian city life or two extras playing a ferocious game of Frisbee without actually tossing a disc, it feels like a uniquely human satire.

During a post-screening Q&A, director and cowriter Jesse Gouldsbury and some members of the creative team shared stories of how difficult it was to get “VelociPastor 2” made. But despite the challenges of filming a microbudget dinosaur movie, it was clear through their laughter that they wouldn’t have it any other way.

“VelociPastor 2” is currently seeking distribution. It’s also in the middle of a series of roadshow screenings. Future dates and locations are listed on the film’s official site .

Watch the “VelociPastor 2” trailer below.

Hollywood）售票一空的特别展映并参与问答环节。这是一个极佳的预热，因为在下个月下旬，奈飞将推出《克里夫·布斯的进一步冒险》（The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth），布拉德·皮特（Brad Pitt）将在大卫·芬奇（David Fincher）执导、改编自昆汀剧本的前传中再度饰演他曾获奥斯卡奖的角色。", "links": [{"text": "Quentin Tarantino will appear", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/10/afi-fest-quentin-tarantino-once-upon-a-time-in-hollywood-1237155933/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本届AFI影展的片单中星光熠熠，囊括了多部奥斯卡热门种子选手，包括探照灯影业（Searchlight）的《Wild Horse Nine》和《Behemoth!》；迈克·李（Mike Leigh）极可能是其最后一部的电影《Tender Loving Care》；弗洛里安·泽勒（Florian Zeller）的《Bunker》；以及由安德鲁·斯科特（Andrew Scott）贡献了备受赞誉表演的《Elsinore》。此外，早期影展宠儿还包括圣丹斯电影节轰动之作、由查宁·塔图姆（Channing Tatum）主演的《Josephine》；以及一部来自柏林、绝对不容错过的发现之作——由导演凯利·奥沙利文（Kelly O'Sullivan）和亚历克斯·汤普森（Alex Thompson）执导的《Mouse》，两人此前还曾打造过圣丹斯备受赞誉的2024年首映佳作《幽灵光》（Ghostlight）。如果你想要个好推荐，千万不要错过《Mouse》。这些电影人是真正的实力派，他们将与其他众多亲临现场的电影人和明星一同出席。本届影展片单还包括10部代表各自国家竞逐国际长片奥斯卡奖的官方选送影片。", "links": [{"text": "International Feature Film Oscar race", "url": "https://deadline.com/lists/oscars-2027-international-feature-film-submissions/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/MAB_3342.jpg?w=300", "alt": "", "caption": "AFI电影节上的鲍勃·加扎莱", "credit": "Deadline · Film", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "借此机会，还有什么比与AFI总裁兼首席执行官鲍勃·加扎莱（Bob Gazzale）交流更好的时机呢？我正是这样做的，以探究他如何看待该电影节在他们的使命中所处的位置，以及在每个奥斯卡季拉开序幕时拥挤不堪的秋季电影节交通堵塞中扮演什么角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "DEADLINE：那么这一切是如何开始的？为什么AFI电影节能够延续下去如此重要，即便有那么多其他争夺注意力的电影节在围剿——更不用说其中一个就举办在业内许多人生活和工作的核心地带？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲍勃·加扎莱：你知道它的历史。AFI电影节建立在加里·埃瑟特（Gary Essert）和加里·亚伯拉罕（Gary Abrahams）通过Filmex打下的无比自豪的基础之上，但当时并没有这样一个电影节……说来也巧，我刚刚看到一段罗纳德·里根（Ronald Reagan）总统欢迎大家参加1987年AFI电影节并为其揭幕的影像。哇！这是一段我从未见过的素材。但这本就是AFI创立的初衷。尽管时代确实变了，明年将迎来AFI成立60周年——那是你我都还记得的年代，当时你看电影是否受限，完全取决于艺术影院的节目策划人，因此AFI的工作就是放映电影。在早期，乔治·史蒂文斯（George Stevens Jr.）在国家美术馆（National Gallery of Art）策划电影，当然还有肯尼迪中心（Kennedy Center），现在则是在银色剧院（Silver Theater）。所以这是我们基因的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但当Filmex遇到一些麻烦时，在洛杉矶举办活动的构想应运而生。尽管世界变了，展映变了，电影——或者无论我们今天怎么称呼它们——变得更容易获取了，但不变的目标依然是将人们聚集在一起、提升各种声音，并且你知道的，提醒人们电影是只有共同体验才能产生共鸣的共同心跳。我的意思是，你可以独自看电影，但没有什么比和一大群人一起看更美妙的了。对我而言，在见证了这么多届电影节顺利举办之后，真正有趣的是，过去两年的AFI电影节似乎成了我们从《深渊》（Obsession）和《后室》（Backrooms）身上所看到的一种先兆，那就是年轻人正在重返影院，千真万确。我们对此的研究表明，这是一种“后疫情”的反弹，人们渴望再次团聚。没有什么地方比银幕折射出的光芒之中更好的了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "DEADLINE：在每年的这个时候，你是如何与众多的其他电影节竞争的？似乎每个人都有一个电影节，而且都想分一杯羹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "GAZZALE：嗯，我们的理念主要是，你知道的，有些影展关注的是“谁是第一”，对吧？而我们的关注点在于“什么是最好”。这是一种非常自由的节目策划方式（托德·希区柯克[Todd Hitchcock]是AFI影展及AFI银色剧院与文化中心的主任）。因为我们不搞“争第一”那一套，而且在好莱坞腹地，你就能领略来自世界各地的顶级佳作，有10部代表各自国家申报奥斯卡奖的影片在此参展。不用坐飞机就能拥有这种体验，正如多萝西（Dorothy）所言，它就近在咫尺，就在你自己的后院里。确实如此。这正是AFI影展的目标，你知道的，做洛杉矶自己的电影节，让你能在此欣赏到来自世界各地以及贯穿全年最优秀的电影。曾有发行商和流媒体给我们打电话说：“嗯，你们可能不想要这个，因为它已经在圣丹斯放映过了。”并非如此。我们赞美圣丹斯。我们赞美所有的电影节都有属于它们的观众，按照我们的理念，多多益善。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "DEADLINE：今年很有意思的一点是，你们的开幕片和闭幕片都与美国电影学会（American Film Institute）有着直接联系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "GAZZALE：关于40周年的另一件事是，它让学会得以——怎么说最好呢——履行其使命，其庞大而多元的使命。我们的开幕片是《Wildwood》，由卡勒德·丹切尔（Caleb Deschanel）掌镜，他正是AFI学院的第一届学员。我们的闭幕片是《Being Heumann》。西恩·海德（Siân Heder）当然是AFI女性导演工作坊的毕业生，她曾被引述说过：“如果没有AFI，我绝不可能成为一名导演。”这里有这么多的校友……感觉这正是40周年所赋予你的能力——培养下一代电影人，然后庆祝他们的作品。我最喜欢的一个关于此的故事是，帕蒂·杰金斯（Patty Jenkins）毕业于AFI，她有一部毕业短片叫《Velocity Rules》，她去参加了AFI影展的一个活动，那是一个与制片人的见面会。她在那里遇到了布拉德·韦曼（Brad Wyman）。她说：“我想拍一部关于连环杀手的电影。”他说：“我们干吧。”他们拍出了《女魔头》（Monster），随后我们在AFI影展举办了世界首映。这就好比将整个AFI融为一体。这是一所源源不断输送杰出人才的电影学校，然后我们有机会在星光灿烂的中国剧院（Chinese Theatre）庆祝他们的成就。哇，这太激动人心了！", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "DEADLINE：今年邀请菲尔·罗德（Phil Lord）和克里斯·米勒（Chris Miller）参与你们的节目策划，这个想法是如何诞生的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "GAZZALE：我们曾与大卫·林奇（David Lynch）、佩德罗·阿尔莫多瓦（Pedro Almodóvar）、阿涅斯·瓦尔达（Agnès Varda）、艾娃·德约麦尼（Ava DuVernay）合作过那么多伟大的艺术家，去年还有吉尔莫·德尔·托罗（Guillermo del Toro）。鉴于当今世界的现状以及外界发生的一切，我问团队谁是最具活力、创意源源不断的团体或电影人，他们给出的答案是罗德和米勒，我说“我们冲吧”，他们答应了。然后当他们提出要放映《2001太空漫游》（2001: A Space Odyssey）时，我说我们要在大中国剧院（big Chinese theater）放映，而不是在小厅（Chinette）。他们兴奋得无以复加，随后当他们推荐了其他电影，包括我深爱的《Harold and Maude》和《里菲奇》（Rififi）——这是最棒最棒的电影——还有《大青蛙影院》（The Muppet Movie）时，我当时就觉得：“这就是治愈良药。”这就是我们为什么要举办电影节的原因，因为如果你有机会观看其中两部、一部、三部或四部电影，你会对自己的生活感觉更好。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第40届AFI影展将于10月21日至25日在好莱坞的TCL中国剧院（TCL Chinese Theatre）举行。", "translated": true}]

present 157 films across five Red Carpet premieres, 12 special screenings, 13 Luminaries selections, 18 Discovery titles, 16 World Cinema selections, 17 documentaries, 45 short films in competition, independently created Filmex before AFI came in, morphing the event into AFI Fest in 1986.", "links": [{"text": "AFI Fest", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/afi-fest/"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Watch on Deadline"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Other Red Carpet galas include Thursday night’s world premiere of Netflix’s Peter Berg-directed, World War II-set movie The Mosquito Bowl; Peter Farrelly’s Oscar Best Picture winner Rocky ‘s origin story I Play Rocky; and the North American premiere of Brad Bird’s ambitious Netflix noir ‘toon Ray Gunn. There will also be an evening devoted to this year’s guest artistic directors, Phil Lord and Chris Miller, who have chosen to present Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 classic 2001: A Space Odyssey in all its glory on the large TCL Chinese Theatre’s Imax screen (appropriate since the pair directed this year’s outer space Oscar contender Project Hail Mary )."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On Friday, Quentin Tarantino will appear for a Q&A following a sold-out special screening of his 2019 epic Los Angeles tale Once Upon a Time in Hollywood , which is a timely primer because late next month Netflix will debut The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth , with Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role in the David Fincher-directed prequel from Tarantino’s script.", "links": [{"text": "Quentin Tarantino will appear", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/10/afi-fest-quentin-tarantino-once-upon-a-time-in-hollywood-1237155933/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The AFI lineup is peppered with a number of Oscar hopefuls including Searchlight’s Wild Horse Nine and Behemoth!; Mike Leigh’s likely final film Tender Loving Care; Florian Zeller’s Bunker; Elsinore, with Andrew Scott’s much praised performance. In addition, early-season festival faves include the Sundance sensation Josephine with Channing Tatum; and a truly not-to-be-missed discovery from Berlin, Mouse, from directors Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson who also did the magnificent 2024 Sundance debut Ghostlight. If you want a good tip don’t miss Mouse. These filmmakers are the real deal and will be among many other filmmakers and stars attending in person. The lineup also includes 10 official country selections for the International Feature Film Oscar race .", "links": [{"text": "International Feature Film Oscar race", "url": "https://deadline.com/lists/oscars-2027-international-feature-film-submissions/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/MAB_3342.jpg?w=300", "alt": "", "caption": "Bob Gazzale AFI Fest", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So on this occasion, what better time than to catch up with AFI President & CEO Bob Gazzale? I did just that to find out where he thinks the fest fits into their mission, as well as the crowded fall-festival traffic jam that kicks off every Oscar season."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "DEADLINE: So how did this all start and why is it so important for AFI Fest to continue, even with the onslaught of so many other festivals competing for attention — not to mention one held right in the heart of where so many in the industry live and work?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "BOB GAZZALE: You know the history of it. The AFI Fest was built on the very proud foundation that Gary Essert and Gary Abrahams built with Filmex, but there was no festival… Oddly, I just saw a film of President Ronald Reagan welcoming everyone to AFI’s 1987 film festival to launch it. Wow! A piece of material I had never seen before. But it’s also what the AFI was built for. And even though times have certainly changed, the founding of AFI was 60 years ago next year — that was back in the day that you and I remember when you were held at the mercy of a programmer at an art house as to whether or not you could see a movie, and so the AFI’s job was to show movies. In the earliest days, it was George Stevens Jr. who programmed films at the National Gallery of Art, and of course at the Kennedy Center, and now at the Silver Theater. So it’s part of our DNA."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But when Filmex ran into a little trouble, the idea of having something in Los Angeles was born, and even though the world has changed, and exhibition has changed, and movies and whatever we call them these days are more accessible, what remains true is the goal is to bring people together and to elevate voices, and you know to remind people that the movies are a common heartbeat that can only be experienced together. I mean you can watch a movie alone, but there’s nothing like watching it with a larger group. And what’s really interesting to me, after watching so many of these roll by, is that the last two years of AFI Fest seem to be kind of a harbinger of what we’re seeing with Obsession and Backrooms , and that is that younger people are going to the movies, that’s true. And our research on this has shown that it’s kind of a post-COVID bounce, where people are eager to be together again. And there’s no better place than in the reflection of a light off a silver screen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "DEADLINE: How do you compete with the multitude of other festivals this time of year? It seems everyone has one, and they all want their piece of the pie."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "GAZZALE: Well, the philosophy is mainly, you know, there are festivals that are focused on what’s first, right? And our focus is on what’s best. And that’s a very freeing way to program (Todd Hitchcock is director of AFI Fest and AFI Silver Theatre and Culture Center). Because we’re not in the game of first, and the idea that right here in the heart of Hollywood you can experience the very best movies from around the world, that there’s 10 films that are being submitted from their countries for Oscar. article_text:
It is a landmark year for the American Film Institute ‘s annual AFI Fest, which is celebrating its 40th anniversary. Opening tonight with the U.S. premiere of Laika’s epic animated feature Wildwood and closing Sunday with Apple’s Being Heumann from Oscar-winning CODA director Siân Heder, this year’s fest will present 157 films across five Red Carpet premieres, 12 special screenings, 13 Luminaries selections, 18 Discovery titles, 16 World Cinema selections, 17 documentaries, 45 short films in competition, 24 films from the AFI Conservatory Showcase, four Guest Artistic Director presentations , three After Dark films … and a partridge in a pear tree.

Related Stories

2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More

Laika’s ‘Wildwood’ To Open AFI Fest 2026

Actually the partridge has not been confirmed to appear, but this lineup right in the heart of Hollywood taking over the TCL Chinese Theatre for five days is quite the ambitious effort that has a rich history, starting with the independently created Filmex before AFI came in, morphing the event into AFI Fest in 1986.

Watch on Deadline

Other Red Carpet galas include Thursday night’s world premiere of Netflix’s Peter Berg-directed, World War II-set movie The Mosquito Bowl; Peter Farrelly’s Oscar Best Picture winner Rocky ‘s origin story I Play Rocky; and the North American premiere of Brad Bird’s ambitious Netflix noir ‘toon Ray Gunn. There will also be an evening devoted to this year’s guest artistic directors, Phil Lord and Chris Miller, who have chosen to present Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 classic 2001: A Space Odyssey in all its glory on the large TCL Chinese Theatre’s Imax screen (appropriate since the pair directed this year’s outer space Oscar contender Project Hail Mary ).

On Friday, Quentin Tarantino will appear for a Q&A following a sold-out special screening of his 2019 epic Los Angeles tale Once Upon a Time in Hollywood , which is a timely primer because late next month Netflix will debut The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth , with Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role in the David Fincher-directed prequel from Tarantino’s script.

The AFI lineup is peppered with a number of Oscar hopefuls including Searchlight’s Wild Horse Nine and Behemoth!; Mike Leigh’s likely final film Tender Loving Care; Florian Zeller’s Bunker; Elsinore, with Andrew Scott’s much praised performance. In addition, early-season festival faves include the Sundance sensation Josephine with Channing Tatum; and a truly not-to-be-missed discovery from Berlin, Mouse, from directors Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson who also did the magnificent 2024 Sundance debut Ghostlight. If you want a good tip don’t miss Mouse. These filmmakers are the real deal and will be among many other filmmakers and stars attending in person. The lineup also includes 10 official country selections for the International Feature Film Oscar race .

So on this occasion, what better time than to catch up with AFI President & CEO Bob Gazzale? I did just that to find out where he thinks the fest fits into their mission, as well as the crowded fall-festival traffic jam that kicks off every Oscar season.

DEADLINE: So how did this all start and why is it so important for AFI Fest to continue, even with the onslaught of so many other festivals competing for attention — not to mention one held right in the heart of where so many in the industry live and work?

BOB GAZZALE: You know the history of it. The AFI Fest was built on the very proud foundation that Gary Essert and Gary Abrahams built with Filmex, but there was no festival… Oddly, I just saw a film of President Ronald Reagan welcoming everyone to AFI’s 1987 film festival to launch it. Wow! A piece of material I had never seen before. But it’s also what the AFI was built for. And even though times have certainly changed, the founding of AFI was 60 years ago next year — that was back in the day that you and I remember when you were held at the mercy of a programmer at an art house as to whether or not you could see a movie, and so the AFI’s job was to show movies. In the earliest days, it was George Stevens Jr. who programmed films at the National Gallery of Art, and of course at the Kennedy Center, and now at the Silver Theater. So it’s part of our DNA.

But when Filmex ran into a little trouble, the idea of having something in Los Angeles was born, and even though the world has changed, and exhibition has changed, and movies and whatever we call them these days are more accessible, what remains true is the goal is to bring people together and to elevate voices, and you know to remind people that the movies are a common heartbeat that can only be experienced together. I mean you can watch a movie alone, but there’s nothing like watching it with a larger group. And what’s really interesting to me, after watching so many of these roll by, is that the last two years of AFI Fest seem to be kind of a harbinger of what we’re seeing with Obsession and Backrooms , and that is that younger people are going to the movies, that’s true. And our research on this has shown that it’s kind of a post-COVID bounce, where people are eager to be together again. And there’s no better place than in the reflection of a light off a silver screen.

DEADLINE: How do you compete with the multitude of other festivals this time of year? It seems everyone has one, and they all want their piece of the pie.

GAZZALE: Well, the philosophy is mainly, you know, there are festivals that are focused on what’s first, right? And our focus is on what’s best. And that’s a very freeing way to program (Todd Hitchcock is director of AFI Fest and AFI Silver Theatre and Culture Center). Because we’re not in the game of first, and the idea that right here in the heart of Hollywood you can experience the very best movies from around the world, that there’s 10 films that are being submitted from their countries for Oscar. That you have the experience without getting on an airplane, that it’s right here in your own backyard, as Dorothy would say. It’s right here. That’s true. That is the goal of AFI Fest, you know, to be L.A.’s film festival, where you can see the very best films from around the world and the very best films from throughout the year. We have had distributors and streamers call us saying, “Well, you probably don’t want this because it’s been at Sundance.” Not true. We celebrate Sundance. We celebrate that all film festivals have their audience, and in our philosophy, the more the merrier.

DEADLINE: It is interesting this year that both your opening-night and closing-night films have a direct connection to the American Film Institute.

GAZZALE: The other thing about 40 years is that it has allowed the institute to, how best say this, fulfill its mandate, its vast and varied mandates. We’re opening with Wildwood which is shot by Caleb Deschanel, who was in the very first class of the AFI Institute. We’re closing with Being Heumann . Siân Heder, of course, is an AFI graduate from the directing workshop for women, who has been quoted as saying, “If it wasn’t for the AFI, I would never be a director.” And there’s so many alums in here… It just feels like that’s what 40 years allows you to do is to train the next generation of filmmakers and then celebrate their work. My favorite story about this is that Patty Jenkins graduated from AFI, and she had a thesis film called Velocity Rules , and she went to an event at AFI Fest where it was a meet-and-greet with producers. And she met Brad Wyman. She said, “I want to make a movie about a serial killer.” He said, “Let’s do it.” They made Monster , and then we had the world premiere at AFI Fest. Like, that’s all of AFI rolled into one. It’s a film school putting out talented people, and then we get the opportunity to celebrate them in the Chinese theater. Wow, what a thrill!

DEADLINE: How did the idea of getting Phil Lord and Chris Miller involved in your programming this year come about?

GAZZALE: We’ve had so many great artists with David Lynch and Pedro Almodóvar and Agnes Varda and Ava DuVernay, and last year with Guillermo del Toro. Given the state of the world today and what’s happening in the exterior, I said to the team who is the most high-energy, endlessly inventive group or filmmaker, and they came back with Lord and Miller, and I said “Let’s go for it,” and they said yes. And then when they came back with 2001: A Space Odyssey , I said we’re showing that in the big Chinese theater, not the Chinette. They were over-the-moon thrilled, and then when they came back with other movies including Harold and Maude and Rififi , which I love — it’s the best best movie. And then The Muppet Movie I was like, “This is the tonic that ails.” This is why we have a film festival because if you have the opportunity to see two or one or three or four of those movies, you’re going to feel better about your life.

The 40th AFI Fest runs October 21 – 25 at TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood.

article_text:
Good news, “ Guardians of the Galaxy ” fans. Chris Pratt , who has played superhero Star-Lord across six films, recently confirmed that his character will return to the MCU and that the studio has already taken “hard action” to make it happen.

“I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been both ongoing conversations about how we make good on that promise and also hard action taken to make sure that we make good on that promise,” said Pratt on The Playlist’s “Bingeworthy” podcast while discussing Star-Lord’s comeback.

Related Stories

Why Olivia Colman Didn’t Get Splinters From Getting Intimate With Alexander Skarsgård's 'Wicker' Costume

Alexander Skarsgård on His Wacky ‘Wicker’ Red Carpet Looks: From Clear Shoes and a Multicolored Skirt to a Gray Wig Inspired by Co-Star Olivia Colman

He continued: “So yeah, you’ll see Star-Lord again, which is very exciting, but I’m not at liberty to say when that’s going to be, but he’s not going anywhere.”

The news comes months after Pratt admitted he pitched Marvel an idea for bringing Star-Lord back into the MCU. “I’m happy to do anything they want me to do and will,” Pratt said about Marvel when on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast. “And also, I personally have a really strong vision of what I would want him to do. And I think it’s fucking great.”

When asked if he pitched this idea already to Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige, Pratt responded: “Yep. And I think that, you know, I’m down to contribute any way I can to them setting up the next 10 years of storytelling, you know? And also, I have a pretty strong idea of how I think I could contribute to that.”

Pratt’s Star-Lord has appeared in “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2,” “Avengers: Infinity War,” “Avengers: Endgame,” “Thor: Love and Thunder” and “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3,” the latter of which promised via credits scene text that Star-Lord would return.

The next installment in the MCU, “Avengers: Doomsday,” hits theaters on Dec. 18.

article_text:
Another day, another film festival. I have been on quite the fall festival tour, starting back in Telluride over Labor Day Weekend, back to Los Angeles for a bit, then the sprawling New York Film Festival, then Middleburg in Virginia, and finally, a festival in another part of this large state, the University of Virginia’s 39-year-old Virginia Film Festival (October 21-25).

This year’s VAFF program offers 100 films and a smattering of starry attendees, including Visionary Award winners Nathan Lane (“The Birdcage”) and Jessica Lange (“Long Day’s Journey Into Night”), interviewed by TCM’s Ben Mankiewicz, as well as writer/director David O. Russell in conversation with Career Producer honoree Todd Black about their upcoming sports film “Madden,” Aaron Sorkin opining about “The Social Reckoning,” and a talk with “The Odyssey” production designer Ruth De Jong, a Charlottesville native.

On the first go-round, it’s fun to navigate new towns (downtown Charlottesville is walkable and charming), tourist attractions (I have not yet checked out Monticello), and complex ticketing systems. The press corps at this festival is slightly less awards -focused than Middleburg (Vanity Fair, Filmmaker Magazine, Vulture, RogerEbert.com, THR, and The Daily Beast among them).

The price of an airplane ticket, hotel room, and access to screenings and talent brings with it the job of introducing movies (in my case, French Oscar entry “Minotaur”) and moderating Q&As (I’m talking to “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” writer/director Tim Blake Nelson). And my “Screen Talk” co-host Ryan Lattanzio and I are welcoming a special guest to a live podcast, “Paper Tiger” director James Gray.

Opening night, the festival showcased Julianne Moore’s Oscar frontrunner performance in “ The Debut ,” which just won Middleburg’s audience award and played just as well for the enthusiastic crowds at the Paramount Theatre, followed by an opening night gala attended by Ilya Tovbis, the festival’s artistic director, and Jody Kielbasa, UVA Vice Provost for the Arts and VAFF Executive Director. “The Debut” also opened well at Woodstock in Upstate New York last week, where Ryan attended and hosted a talk with “The Liberation” star Carrie Coon and writer/director Guy Nattiv.

The VAFF lineup is chock full of the usual awards suspects, from “La Bola Negra” and “Behemoth!” and “Being Heumann” to “14th,” “Club Kid,” “Wild Horse Nine,” and “Elsinore.”

title_original: ‘Desiring Machines’ Dares Us to Imagine a Healthy Relationship with Technology
editorial_title_zh: 《欲望机器》：挑战我们去想象与科技的健康关系

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这就是在阿根廷马德普塔当代艺术博物馆展出的新展“欲望机器”的核心问题。在这样一个时代，未来似乎可以从技术进步不可阻挡的步伐中清晰读出，策展人奥古斯蒂娜·里纳尔迪（Augustina Rinaldi）借助哲学家吉尔·德勒兹（Gilles Deleuze）和费利克斯·加塔利（Felix Guattari）的著作提出了另一种主张：塑造社会转型的不是创新，而是欲望，因此，只有通过理解我们的欲望，我们才可能创造出新的、意想不到的未来。该展览展出了10位阿根廷艺术家作品，展期至11月2日。一进入展厅，人便有一种步入实验室的感觉。有机材料和无机材料在一个充满可能与发明的受控、无菌环境中交织在一起。《呼出颤抖的装置》（2025），塞莱斯特·马丁内斯·阿布拉（Celeste Martinez Abburra）的大型雕塑，明确让人联想到化学实验室的不锈钢和玻璃烧杯。由金属悬挂并通过管道连接的精致玻璃器皿收集冷凝水，水滴落入一池恶臭的水中。在华金·法尔加斯（Joaquin Fargas）的《生物圈项目》（2006-2026）中，浮在密封地球仪中的水生植物安装在一个呈蜘蛛状的铬金属钳子三脚架上。其他地方的两件录像作品反映了里纳尔迪策展营造的诡异、冰冷的氛围，试图捕捉现实与未来之间的“中间地带”，正如墙面文字所说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": Harte）的“Danza”系列（2025），由一片充满油性质感金属形态的幽灵般的树桩森林组成；或者异形藤蔓侵入其裂缝。这是一个令人不安的画面：完整而有机的部分被技术触手穿透，这反映了我们自己与设备以及产生它们的权力基础设施之间无可救药地交织在一起的关系。德勒兹和加塔利的著作为理解这些位于有机体与机器之间令人不安的谱系上的穿透性雕塑提供了有用的语境。展览标题借用了他们1972年的著作《反俄狄浦斯：资本主义与精神分裂症》，他们在书中对弗洛伊德的精神分析理论发起了攻击，该理论认为欲望源于缺失，以及他相关的“俄狄浦斯情结”，即提出无意识是由乱伦的浪漫竞争构成的——或者正如德勒兹和加塔利所说，“爸爸-妈妈-我”的三位一体。他们对欲望的理解是，它不是由缺乏产生的，而是通过任何形式的关系产生的，包括一个人与物的关系。作者提出了对欲望的更为系统的理解，即将其视为有机机器中的一个齿轮，无限地与其他机器发生反应。", article_text:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot , a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet. The column will appear every other Monday.

A classic illustration of a world that has fallen to technology first appeared on Facebook in the 2010s and has been circulating online ever since. You likely know it: Rows of bent heads gazing at their phone screens; each face replaced by a ray of light sucked towards the screen. By 2026, the illustration has become boomer meme par excellence, but it captures the familiar feeling that our relationship with technology is one-sided, hypnotic, and vampiric. AI-induced existential panic has only heightened this feeling, leading to a keen desire to set some boundaries with our devices.

Cue the Instagram infographics on how to develop analog hobbies; viral videos of young people simply socializing without their phones, digital detox camps , and the under 13 social media bans . Cue the paranoia that every so-called analog activity is inherently performative, such as reading in public . But what if these measures were misguided? What if instead of punishing ourselves for our technological entanglements, we got curious?

That’s the question at the center of “Desiring Machines” a new exhibition on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Mar del Plata, Argentina. At a time when it seems that the future can be clearly read in the inevitable march of technological advancement, curator Augustina Rinaldi leans on the work of philosophers’ Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari to make an alternative claim: it is not innovation but desire which shapes social transformation, and thus, it is only by understanding our desires that we might generate new and unexpected futures. The exhibition feature ten Argentine artists and is on view until November 2. Upon entering, one has the feeling of having entered into a laboratory. Organic and inorganic materials mingle in a controlled, sterile environment pregnant with possibility and invention. Device for Exhaling the Tremor (2025), a large sculpture by Celeste Martinez Abburra, explicitly recalls the stainless steel and glass beakers of a chemistry laboratory. Delicate glass vessels suspended by metal and connected by pipes gather condensation that drips into a pool of fetid water. In Joaquin Fargas’s Biosphere Project (2006-2026), aquatic plants floating in sealed globes are installed on a tripod of spidery, chrome pincers. Two video works elsewhere reflect the uncanny, cold environment Rinaldi has curated in an attempt to capture, “an intermediate horizon” between the present and the future, as as per the wall text.

You Will Become Salt (2024) by Indira Montoya is set in the state of Córdoba hundreds of years after its inundation in a series of floods. Using photogammetry, a technique which renders 2D surfaces into 3D models, and game engines, Montoya directs a virtual drone that hovers over the ruins of cities and its strange, frozen residents. Celeste Martínez Aburrá’s film Cartography of the Infra-Thin (2025), also set in Córdoba, features a white field covered in snow where the artist has installed a series of smoke machines. The camera flies through this bizarre set of ice and vapor.

Facing this is Miguel Harte’s “Danza” series (2025), consisting of a ghostly forest of tree stumps bursting with oily, metallic forms; or alien vines invading their crevices. It’s an uncomfortable image: what is whole and organic has been penetrated by the technological tentacle, mirroring our own hopelessly enmeshed relationship with our devices and the infrastructures of power which produce them. The work of Deleuze and Guattari provides a useful context to understand these penetrative sculptures that sit on a discomfiting spectrum of organism and machine. The title of the exhibition is borrowed from their 1972 book “Anti-Oedipus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia” in which they mount an attack on both Freud’s psychoanalytic theory that desire stems from absence, and his related “Oedipus complex” which proposes that the unconscious is structured by an incestuous romantic rivalry—or as Deleuze and Guattari put it, the “daddy-mommy-me” trinity. Their understanding of desire is that it is not produced by lack but through any form of relation, including one’s relation to objects. The authors propose a more systemic understanding of desire as one cog in an organic machine, infinitely reacting to other machines.

Consider Martina Servio Olavide’s sculptural installation Untitled (2025). The work consists of a transparent female figure, sculpted with her back arched in a bridge position and filled halfway with water. She has no arms, and is surrounded by small, round mirrors. Her mannequin head is serene, but a set of external ribs peek out from underneath like the bony grip of a witch. The living element in the objectified shell, the splayed offering before a set of mirrors which both reflect her and the audience. One reading of Untitled is as a diagram of how desire shapes our perception of one another and of ourselves. Even more, how that gaze is projected online.

The work doesn’t condemn social media, but rather withholds the predictable interpretation (it’s all objectification!), forcing viewers in for a closer look. Whether it’s the “Danza” series or the Biospheres Project , the works on view push us to consider that a flat rejection of technology is an overly simplistic reaction. If we confront the desire perpetuating these terrifying enmeshments, we might become capable of imagining a more creative future for these relationships.

In other words, desire, in an unrepressed form, explodes the channels through which it is expected to flow. Here, art works to excite a deeper perception of where our desire is being frustrated or forcibly channeled, and where it might flow if the dam broke. What might emerge if that desire was unleashed? “Desiring Machines” is not a diorama of the future. It is a snapshot of a process perpetually in motion. Our dance with objects, and through those objects, how we dance with each other.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Jay Roach and longtime producing partner Michelle Graham are on board to produce a new female-driven ensemble comedy for New Line, Deadline has learned.

The film’s title and plot are being kept under wraps for now. Larry Stuckey & Joanna Leeds are adapting the screenplay from a story they conceived with Joanna’s brother, Andrew Leeds . The project reunites Roach with Stuckey, who began his film career as a development exec for Roach before associate producing and contributing to the writing of his iconic comedy Meet the Fockers and co-writing follow-up Little Fockers .

Related Stories

New Line Wins Heated Bidding War For Theo James Krekis Horror Package 'Jealous People Are Ugly People'

'The Mummy' Review: Lee Cronin's Reimagining Is Plenty Fiendish But Too Wrapped Up In Imitation

Roach returns to New Line after directing the Austin Powers trilogy for the studio. His extensive filmography also includes comedies like Meet the Parents , Meet the Fockers and The Campaign , as well as such prestige dramas as Trumbo and Bombshell , which received a combined four Oscar nominations, with Bombshell winning one. Roach also earned major accolades for directing the political dramas Recount , Game Change and All the Way . Additional producing credits include The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy , Sisters and Borat . His most recent projects include directing the Searchlight film The Roses , starring Benedict Cumberbatch and Olivia Colman, and producing Focker-In-Law , the latest installment in the Fockers franchise starring Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro and Ariana Grande, which is out November 25. He is repped by UTA, Mosaic and Behr Abramson Levy Johnson.

Watch on Deadline

Joanna Leeds created and stars in the series Bulldozer , which premiered at Sundance and went on to win the Audience Award at SXSW. She also appears in the latest season of Monster and recurs on HBO’s Rooster . She is repped by 3 Arts Entertainment and Toczek Suddleson.

An Emmy-nominated actor, writer and director, Andrew Leeds wrote and directed the Bulldozer pilot and has written and produced pilots for ABC, NBC, CBS, Fox and Showtime. His acting credits include The Patient , Zoey’s Extraordinary Playlist and Barry . He is repped by Gersh, Perennial Entertainment and Toczek Suddleson.

Stuckey is repped by 3 Arts and Gendler, Kelly & Cunningham.
